lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the state and the factory
lead.head: The way station that wasn’t
body: Is manufacturing something special, or is it just like anything else? In the second of two episodes on manufacturing, Ajay Shah gave his answer early: “There’s nothing special about manufacturing.”

He had been irritated by the opposite view for thirty years, he said. Development economists, in his opening words, are “a bit of a creepy bunch”, statist control people with a “smug comfort and superiority complex that they get to control the world”. {105-J02}
Amit Varma reported that before the shoot his co-host had been a volcano. On camera he was “a flickering candle”, though the light, Varma promised, would still come through.
## How the dogma was built
Shah began with the development economics of the 1960s, 70s and 80s, which rested on four ideas.
Nicholas Kaldor saw that countries with fast GDP growth tended to have fast manufacturing growth. Wright’s Law, the experience curve, was said to work only in factories.

Albert O. Hirschman argued that one factory sparks many others through linkages, so the state should get a few going. Hollis Chenery’s World Bank data showed successful countries passing through a phase of heavy manufacturing before becoming services economies.
Together they hardened into dogma. “Every development success will go through this script,” Shah said. “It is seen as a necessary way station, and then you can graduate to other things.” {105-C01}
The trouble began, he argued, when economists were willing to use state power to fake that stage.
## What went wrong
It did not work, for two reasons. Hirschman was right about linkages, Shah said, but they went global: a German car now carries Czech seats, Romanian wiring and software from Pune.
And picking winners fails, between firms or between sectors. “There is a role for the state, which is to lay foundations and then be neutral,” he said. {105-C05}

Varma insisted that the hosts were not against manufacturing. Their quarrel was with coercion: a state that declares one path to growth and forces the economy down it, leaving a poor country poor for longer.

India, Shah said, is “ground zero” where the old theory is being destroyed. Over ten years its goods exports grew 38 per cent in nominal dollars, while services exports grew 126 per cent. Fibre-optic cables, he argued, have made services more tradable than goods. {105-C08}
## Umpires and lychees

The hosts tested the argument on Bombay’s stalled bid to become a financial centre, where trust in institutions matters more than technology, and on food, where the Netherlands, the size of Haryana, is the world’s third-largest exporter.

What the state owes everyone, Shah said again and again, is peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice. “If you will do peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice, we’ve got a lot done.”

Why does the old dogma survive? Varma blamed the lag between the world and those who think about it. “The map of the world is always out of date,” he said; in the world of intellectual constructs, it is “much more out of date than you would otherwise expect”. {105-C14}
Shah’s lessons for young economists were two. Be very cautious about correlation and causality. And distrust any leadership role for the state in choosing society’s path.
Then he recommended the books of the very man he had spent the episode criticising. Hirschman, Shah said, was “one of the great people”.

second.label: Inside the ministry
second.head: Target practice
second.deck: Ajay Shah asked who exports, and was told to grow up
body: Soon after Ajay Shah joined the Ministry of Finance, he sat in on the annual meeting where officials set India’s export target. He asked the room an awkward question: who in this room does any exporting? {105-S01}

Exporting is done by private people, he pointed out. The government’s target, he argued, should be the rules it got out of the way so that those people could export, not a guess at how much they would sell.

Amit Varma wanted to know whether he got a spanking. Not quite. The officials treated him like a *naadaan baalak*, a naive child, and told him that when he grew up and became a real policymaker, he would understand the importance of targets. {#baalak}

quote.text: Exporting is done by private people. Who are people in this room to make up a target?

second.caption: the export-target meeting

third.head: Ploughing by telemetry
body: There is no longer a clear line between manufacturing and services, Ajay Shah said. {105-C07} Rolls-Royce does not sell engines; it bills by the engine-hour and handles maintenance, finance and insurance.

A John Deere tractor downloads firmware, probes the soil and sends data to a call centre in Hyderabad, which phones the farmer about an infestation. “The tractor is now a sensor platform,” Shah said. {#sensor}
His mentor Kirit Parikh explained the rise of services long ago: “Once you have enough food to eat, you want the best chef to make the food. And that’s services.”
Amit Varma had a question of his own: if you are a man who gets turned on by farm vehicles, what would those vehicles be called? Shah’s verdict: “Brilliant.” {105-J03}

sections.label: The old view
sections.head: Four pillars and a dogma
sections.caption: the four pillars of the old dogma
body: Before tearing the theory down, Ajay Shah built it up. The development economics of the 1960s, 70s and 80s, he said, rested on four pillars, and their history matters.
The first was Nicholas Kaldor’s. In the 1950s, Kaldor observed that successful countries which got GDP growth tended to get manufacturing growth. Shah called it “a crude correlation”. {105-J09}

The second was Wright’s Law, the experience curve: the more you do something, the better you get. Economists claimed it happened only in manufacturing. Produce ten raised to eight ball bearings, and you have walked a long way down the cost curve.
## Candles and surges

The third was Albert O. Hirschman’s linkages. One factory buys raw materials and sets the stage for others, so the state should get “a couple of these candles going” and let capitalist incentives fill in the rest. Hirschman called it unbalanced growth.

The fourth was Hollis Chenery’s structural transformation. Working with the first high-quality multi-country data at the World Bank, he and his co-authors found successful countries surging to “twenty forty fifty per cent of GDP as manufacturing” before becoming services economies. {#surge}

~ Together the four ideas crystallised into dogma: agriculture must decline, manufacturing must rise, and services are not important. Many development economists then wanted state power to induce the stage. That, Shah said, is “crossing a huge line”. {105-C01}

quote.text: It is seen as a necessary way station, and then you can graduate to other things.

sections.label: Mugged by reality
sections.head: There is no German car
sections.caption: why linkages went global
body: The theory sounded convincing, Amit Varma said, but practice did not turn out as its economists expected. Ajay Shah gave two reasons.

First, Hirschman was “completely right on linkages, but the linkages went all over the world”. There is no German car: its seats are made in the Czech Republic, its wiring in Romania and its operating-system software by KPIT in Pune. {105-C02}

So the cure is to remove every friction against integrating with the world: passports, visas, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, the Enforcement Directorate, cross-border payments, and current and capital account restrictions.
## Picking winners
Second, picking winners does not work. The state should fix what hobbles manufacturing and what hobbles agriculture, Shah said, but must never rank sectors like a central planner. {105-C05}

Varma added a clarification: the hosts were not against manufacturing. Their quarrel was with a state that uses coercion to favour one path to growth, which “leaves a poor country poorer” for far longer.

~ Subsidies only fake it, Shah argued. Rig the exchange rate and the most incompetent manufacturer in India looks globally competitive. “If you subsidise something, it will grow. But that’s not growth.” {105-C04}

quote.text: Cars are made all over the world and there is no country anymore.

sections.label: The new model
sections.head: Only the high-skilled game
sections.caption: the high-skilled game
body: If the old model is delusional, Amit Varma asked, what is the new one? Ajay Shah’s first answer: the vast factory full of unskilled villagers is over.
Modern manufacturing runs on automation and capital: computer numerically controlled lathes, programmed by English speakers who read the manuals and watch YouTube guides.

It also demands discipline. “People have to come to work at 9 a.m. and they have to work correctly for eight hours,” Shah said, because hundreds share an assembly line. {#nine} He sees a real problem with young Indian men: a culture of machismo, violence, alcohol and late nights.
## Goods or services?
Second, the line between manufacturing and services has dissolved. Rolls-Royce bills by the engine-hour, and a John Deere tractor reports on the soil to a call centre in Hyderabad.

Third, services are now more tradable than goods. When Shah was young, his father told him that haircuts are not tradable while widgets are. {#father} Fibre-optic cables changed that: an exchange in Chicago takes orders from the whole world.

~ So India is “ground zero”. Over ten years its goods exports grew 38 per cent in nominal dollars, about half a per cent a year after US inflation. {#halfpercent} Services exports grew 126 per cent. “This is a miracle,” Shah said.

quote.text: There is only a high-skilled game that is available, and we have to play that game.

sections.label: The Bombay dream
sections.head: Stadiums don’t make umpires
sections.caption: umpires, not stadiums
body: Ajay Shah’s test case was Bombay’s bid to become an international financial centre, a dream that began with a question from Jaswant Singh when he was Finance Minister. {105-S02}

The first stage is already here, he said. Global firms such as JP Morgan employ huge numbers of English-speaking Indians to support work done in London and New York. Selling a financial product made in India to the world is far harder.

A buyer of dollar-yen futures is exposed, for the life of the contract, to everything about the system that stands behind it. {105-C09} That is why Percy Mistry told Shah that good technology was nowhere near enough.
## The umpire test
Build the world’s best stadiums at Wankhede or Brabourne, Shah said, and the best teams still won’t come if the umpires are “thora shady”. {105-C10}
The British, he said, organised Wimbledon, and foreigners always win at Wimbledon. Britain built the rules of the game and won the world’s trust that its common law will deliver. {105-J15}

~ Amit Varma called it invisible infrastructure. Shah added norms: umpires and judges behave better when their friends ask what on earth they were doing, or when researchers criticise their orders. Varma hurried to say that Indian umpires are the best umpires.

quote.text: It’s not the technical characteristics of the stadium. The umpires are key.

sections.label: Food
sections.head: Lychees for Tokyo
sections.caption: the Netherlands and its food exports
body: Before lunch, Amit Varma asked for a story about food, and Ajay Shah offered a number. The Netherlands, the area of Haryana or Kerala, is the world’s third-largest food exporter, at $140 billion a year. {105-C12}
Agriculture, Shah said, is a site of productivity growth like any other: indoor farming, agricultural robots, genetic engineering, run by highly skilled people rather than unskilled peasants.
## Paid for complexity

The world economy pays for complexity, he argued. Grow wheat “under the benign influence of the PDS” and you will not be paid much. Transporting lychees from Bihar to Tokyo is complex, and private people, not the government, worked out that trade. {#lychee}
India is already partly there. Its food exports, about $43 billion, exceed its textile and apparel exports of $34 billion. {#food43}
Varma recalled the farmer leader Sharad Joshi’s couplet on the APMC monopolies, which squeezed farmers and consumers at once. {105-S05}

~ The Netherlands reminded Varma of Iceland, which drew one-all with Argentina at the 2018 World Cup with a population, he calculated, the size of Versova. “Iceland is three hundred thousand fishermen,” Shah said.

quote.text: Agriculture is only low grade if your imagination is low grade.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah spent the episode criticising Albert O. Hirschman’s work on linkages, then urged everyone to read his books and his biography, Jeremy Adelman’s *Worldly Philosopher*. Hirschman, Shah said, “led the world’s best life”. {105-R02}

contQuote.text: Umpires are not made just by law. They’re made by people. They’re made by respect. An umpire should feel embarrassed when they go home in the evening and their friends say to them, What the hell were you doing?

stories.caption: the dream of Bombay as a financial centre
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a minister’s question and a stalled dream
stories.head: Bombay’s long game against London
body: The idea did not come from the economists. When Jaswant Singh was Finance Minister, Ajay Shah recalled, he sat with Rakesh Mohan and Shah and asked whether they had thought about Bombay as a global producer of financial services. {105-S02}
“I know this will take twenty-five years,” the minister said, as Shah tells it, “but you have to play for twenty-five years. And Bombay must challenge London.”

London makes immense amounts of GDP as the world’s financial centre. The question led to a government committee headed by Shah’s friend Percy Mistry, whose report, *Bombay as an International Financial Centre*, came out in 2007. {#report}

The raw material, Shah said, was already there. JP Morgan has perhaps 60,000 people in India. {#jpmorgan} Throw a stone at any residential building in Bombay, he said, and you will hit some derivatives trader, while people in coffee shops strike complex financial deals.

What was missing was correct financial regulation and a city fit to live in. A great financial centre needs 100,000 expats in the world’s best-paid jobs to relocate there, and police stations that can deal with them in English. {#expats}
The work led to FSLRC and a draft law. “But then everything got derailed,” Shah said.
~ Some 25 years after the minister’s question, he thinks the job has passed on. The next generation, he said, must pick up the pieces and build a Bombay “that you would like to live in”.
stories.why: One good question from a minister can launch a reform that runs for decades, and it can stall just as easily. The hosts tell how Indian finance got stuck in an earlier episode, *The Journey of Indian Finance*. {105-R12}
stories.postscript: Shah, on Bombay’s traders, to Varma: “I know you hang out with the people who do conversations about poker.” {105-J04}

stories.start: Percy taught me this. Percy said the quality of the financial product
stories.end: And it was Percy who showed us this complexity and this richness.
stories.caption: Percy Mistry’s lesson
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the lesson Percy Mistry taught him
stories.head: The microphone and the promise
body: As a young man, Ajay Shah was proud that NSE had the best computer technology in the world, and thought it was ready to serve customers everywhere. Percy Mistry stopped him: “No, hold on, you need much more.” {105-S03}
Take a microphone, Shah said, like the one on the table. Once it is made and tested, nobody cares where it came from.

A financial product is different. Hold a two-month dollar-yen futures position in Chicago and, for those two months, you depend on a whole machinery of private institutions, regulators and law. “Percy said the quality of the financial product is the quality of its institutional environment.” {105-C09}
~ NSE once had a real edge in technology, Shah said. Today the West has caught up.
stories.why: Technology is not the moat in financial services; institutions are. A financial product is a promise that lasts over time, and buying it means trusting the country that stands behind it.

stories.end: you have to take twenty five years to rebuild that confidence and that goodwill
stories.caption: the 2019 payment delay
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the day NSE was late with payments
stories.head: One bad day, twenty-five years
body: In 2019, foreign participants on NSE faced a payment delay because of what Ajay Shah called “some stupid dispute between NSE and SEBI”. Jayanth R Varma wrote about it on his blog. {105-S04}
Reading it, Shah remembered Percy Mistry’s lesson all over again. “You can’t have a payment failure at NSE,” he said. “It doesn’t matter why it happened.”
The show must go on, he argued. Under no circumstances do you delay a payment to a customer, least of all a foreign one, and SEBI and NSE need the capability to make sure of it.
~ On that day, the foreigner decides that payments cannot be trusted to come correctly out of an Indian exchange. Rebuilding that goodwill, Shah said, can take twenty-five years. {#goodwill}
stories.why: Trust in financial infrastructure takes decades to build and one bad day to lose. Whatever the quarrel inside, an institution needs the competence to keep paying its customers, and to keep the show going.

stories.end: my produce cheap and die. You pay too much and you die too
stories.caption: Sharad Joshi’s couplet
stories.kicker: Amit Varma recalls the farmer leader Sharad Joshi
stories.head: Cheap to sell, dear to buy
body: As the talk turned to food, Amit Varma recalled the farmer leader Sharad Joshi, one of the post-independence politicians he truly admires, “because he cared about freedom”. {#joshi}
Joshi took aim at the APMCs. Granted a monopoly by the state, Varma said, they could buy from the farmer at one rupee and sell to the consumer at twenty rupees, and neither had a choice.
Joshi summed it up in a *sher*, spoken from a farmer to a consumer: “Marte hum bhi hain, marte tum bhi ho. Hum sasta bech ke marte hain, tum mehenga khareed ke marte ho.” {105-S05}
~ Varma translated: “I die, my friend, and so do you. I sell my produce cheap and die. You pay too much and you die too.”
stories.why: A middleman’s monopoly granted by the state does not trade the farmer off against the consumer. It hurts both at once, and one couplet says what pages of policy analysis argue.
stories.postscript: Varma has made the case himself in an article, *The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer*.

quiz.q: Which four ideas, in Ajay Shah’s telling, hardened into the old manufacturing dogma?
quiz.a: Kaldor’s laws of growth, Wright’s Law, Hirschman’s linkages and Chenery’s structural transformation.

quiz.q: Where, according to Ajay Shah, does a ‘German’ car get its operating-system software?
quiz.a: From KPIT in Pune; the seats come from the Czech Republic.

quiz.q: What did the officials at the export-target meeting treat Ajay Shah as?
quiz.a: A naadaan baalak: a naive child who would understand targets once grown up.

quiz.q: What does Rolls-Royce sell its customers, according to Ajay Shah, if not engines?
quiz.a: An engine as a service, billed by the hour, with maintenance and insurance.

quiz.q: Over ten years, how much did India’s services exports grow, against its goods exports?
quiz.a: Services exports grew 126 per cent; goods exports grew just 38 per cent.

quiz.q: What is Ajay Shah’s ‘metric for goodness’, as Amit Varma revealed it?
quiz.a: The fraction of *Everything is Everything* episodes you have watched, from zero to one.
